beats.trigger: ## From Personal to Team
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: You can't really share an agent.
beats.got: You don't hand a colleague an agent. You hand over a piece of it, and which piece is a choice I make.

beats.trigger: **Bring one example from your own organisation where people got access to a tool and did not use it.**
beats.got: I already have this example. The learning portal we rolled out two years ago, which about a fifth of people opened.

beats.trigger: **Find** the absorption bottleneck and draft the technical plan and the people plan together
beats.got: There's a people plan next to the technical plan. Good, though 'absorption bottleneck' is jargon I haven't had explained yet.

beats.trigger: What would you want a teammate to have: your `memory/` folder, one of your skills, the morning output, or a way to ask the agent a question in Slack?
beats.got: I'm asked to choose between four things I can't picture yet. I have no memory folder or skills, so I'm guessing at what they are.

beats.trigger: Start with the teammate's work, not with *"what should I share with my teammate?"*
beats.got: Start from the colleague's job, not from my tool. That is how I already think about role design.

beats.trigger: This is a heavy read across the working set.
beats.got: The agent reads my files and writes down a teammate's job. I'm unsure it can know their job from my files, and I'd rather ask the person.

beats.trigger: If the reason is *"we already have the platform,"* send it back.
beats.got: Choosing a tool because we already own it is the mistake I see in HR tech all the time. The four options are clear enough.

beats.trigger: [Design the sharing plan](design-the-sharing-plan.md) finds what would stop that candidate from being absorbed
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Find the obstacle that decides whether the teammate can absorb it, then draft both halves of the plan.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The obstacle is usually not the first technical limitation a builder sees.
beats.got: The real blocker is usually a social or trust issue, not a technical one. 'Absorption' is the word I wasn't given earlier.

beats.trigger: A polished technical file beside a people file full of unnamed roles is the finding, not a finished rollout.
beats.got: If the people plan has no names in it, the plan isn't done, however good the technical side looks. I'd put that in front of my own leadership team.

beats.trigger: checks the assumptions underneath these plans, imagines the failure, and writes the first real-world contact to `module-7/monday.md`.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The technical and people plans are hypotheses.
beats.got: The plans are guesses until a person has reacted to them.

beats.trigger: what would have to be true for this teammate, doing this job, to fire their current hire and use my candidate?
beats.got: I ask what would have to be true for them to switch, instead of how to get them to adopt. 'Fire their current hire' is an odd phrase to use about people's work, but I see the point.

beats.trigger: Six months from now, the teammate went back to the incumbent.
beats.got: Imagining the failure first is a pre-mortem, and it ends in one person and one question for Monday. That is something I could actually do.

beats.trigger: A candidate picked because it fits the infrastructure is shopping. A candidate picked because it moves the outcome is design.
beats.got: Choose by the outcome the person needs, not by what the platform supports. That applies to every HR system we buy.

beats.trigger: ## Lecture: Access is not absorption
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The two get reported as one number and they are not one thing.
beats.got: Licences handed out and tools actually used get reported as one number, and they are different things. That is my learning portal exactly.

beats.trigger: The proposal got neither a yes nor a no.
beats.got: A real failure told plainly: the analysis was done and nobody decided. It reads as honest, and I have lived through the same pattern with change negotiations.

beats.trigger: Accountability is the part with a name on it, and a name does not travel inside a folder.
beats.got: You can copy an agent's context, limits and checks, but not the person who answers for it. Someone has to own it, and that is a people question.

beats.trigger: Pick the one your teammate's week can take in.
beats.got: Each of the four ways to share asks something different of the receiver, so I match it to their week. That is the question I'd take to my HR partners.

beats.trigger: Your candidate is not competing with nothing. It is competing with that.
beats.got: The thing I'm introducing competes with whatever they do today, even if that is a spreadsheet or a habit. This repeats the earlier exercise.

beats.trigger: Have the conversation before you build anything more.
beats.got: Talk to one person before building anything more. It is small and I can do it.

beats.trigger: Who gets your context, who gets a skill, who wants only the output, and who would use an @mention?
beats.got: I sort my colleagues by which kind of sharing suits them. It is a sensible question, but I'd mostly be guessing.

beats.trigger: Access is a switch someone flips. Absorption happens in other people's weeks.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Their answer is the evidence. The plan is still the hypothesis.
beats.got: What the person says is the evidence and my plan is only a guess. I like that it keeps me modest.

beats.trigger: ## Next
beats.got: nothing new

take_homes: Access and absorption are different. We have handed out tools before, and counting licences tells us nothing about use.
When I want a colleague to use something, I start from their job and ask what would have to be true for them to switch, not how to get them to adopt it.
The people plan needs names (who owns it, who answers for it) as much as the technical plan does. Every agent has a person behind it, and that person does not copy.

monday.move: Ask one of my HR business partners how she prepares the weekly people-metrics summary today, and what would make her switch. I would not build anything yet.
monday.who: One HR business partner I trust
monday.stop_condition: If she says the current way works well enough and sees no gain, I drop the idea for now.
monday.blocker: Employee data in an AI tool needs the works council and the DPO, and I haven't asked either yet. I'd keep the first conversation to how she does the job today, with no real data.

misconception.why: The module never talks about headcount, so I still carry the question into the leadership meeting. But the story shows that a capable agent system produced a proposal and nobody decided, and the point about accountability shows that the human side is the slow part. That makes 'which roles go first' look less like the main question. I now think the more pressing question is who owns and absorbs the work.

one_line: Short on tools and long on the human side: access is easy, absorption is the hard part, and I came away with one conversation to have on Monday.
